275	  reuse and mints a fresh one nightly. Measured 2026-07-29/30: **eleven of twelve consumers frozen
276	  on the 2026-07-28 canon ref, 27 orphan `claudinite/maintenance-*` branches, several repos
277	  carrying two for one day** — and every nightly run green throughout. Nothing detected it; the
278	  owner did, by feel ("I feel the situation is bad"). Two habits follow. Read the status of every
279	  API write whose result you then branch on — a body-only destructure turns a refusal into a
280	  plausible object. And judge the fleet by **members' stamps**, never by scheduler run
281	  conclusions: the stamp is the only artifact that moves when baselining actually worked, which is
282	  why a stamp-staleness alarm (#331) is the missing guard and not a nice-to-have.
283	- **A fleet task's target list is enumerated dynamically; the routine's reachable-repo grant is
284	  hand-typed UI config — they drift, and the drift completes rather than fails.** The precondition
285	  builds its member list over `FLEET_GITHUB_TOKEN` (`engine/scheduler/signals/fleet.mjs`, "the one
286	  token that can enumerate every repo the owner owns"), while the executor routine's MCP repo scope
287	  is set by hand in a UI no Action can read — so every member adopted from here on is enumerated by
288	  the precondition and invisible to the executor until someone widens the grant, and the gap only
289	  ever widens. Measured 2026-07-31 on #602: the dispatch named 12 members, the session's grant
290	  listed 10, and `growth-promote` reads members **over the API, never a checkout** — so the run
291	  would have noted two denials, proceeded, and filed a PR reading as a complete 12-member sweep.
292	  That is the worse of the two failure shapes: a routing mismatch stalls visibly (nothing happens,
293	  forever, and you notice), an unreachable target *succeeds wrongly*. So a fleet task must **fail
294	  loudly on a Context target it cannot reach** rather than proceed on a partial list, and adopting a
295	  member is not done until the routine's repo scope names it. No check can catch either half — this
296	  is routine config, not repo content.

=== e27e397 static-website pack: date-anchored versions, release-on-push, explicit publish set (#611)
Two halves of one standard for our static-site repos (Refs #609).

The version scheme becomes v<major>.<ymmdd>.<n>: ymmdd is the last digit of the
UTC year then MMDD, so the ordering that the bare MMDD form broke across a year
boundary (1.1231.3 sorted above the next day's 1.0101.1) holds again —
1.61231.3 -> 1.70101.1. n is the day's release counter, and the major absorbs
the decade wrap (1.91231.4 -> 2.00101.1) so it holds forever; any other
decrease is a version dated in the future and fails the bump loudly. The scheme
and the code that computes it live in one file, the vendored bump action, which
the checks import from rather than restating.

The pack carries the whole flow: an orchestrator that releases on push to main,
reusable publish and Pages-deploy workflows, a PR gate (conformance sweep +
the repo's tests + an artifact-assembly dry run), and three composite actions —
authored once in stubs/ and vendored into each site repo's own .github/, kept
byte-current there by a standing vendoring migration record.

The published artifact is an EXPLICIT list — publish_paths under publish_root
in the repo's required .github/site.config — not the repo root minus the dirs
we remember to hide: a subtractive rule publishes every file nobody thought to
exclude, and publishes each new one silently. Assembly fails on a publish path
that does not exist and on a site with no index.html, on the PR as well as on
the deploy.

Adoption asks the two things the pack cannot default: where the site is served
(Pages, or elsewhere — in which case none of the deploy machinery is vendored
and every rule here stays inert) and what is published. The repo settings that
only a human can turn on are tracked as a one-time issue in the adopting repo,
not as a repo file.

=== b56a15c Prove a canon change is safe for consumers: self-test, rehearsal, canary, and the rule (#595)
* engine: a startup self-test — can Claudinite run here?

Deliberately not a conformance check. check_the_world judges the repo's
CONTENT against the rules; this judges whether the MACHINERY that would run
those rules is intact. A repo can be perfectly conformant and still have a
broken mount, a hook pointing at a deleted file, or a pack the loader
silently drops — and none of that is visible to a content check, because a
rule that never runs reports nothing.

Every fleet-wide failure this corpus has had was that shape, and each is a
probe here:

  #397  inject-pack-prose imported a module that did not exist, so every
        active pack's RULES.md went un-injected fleet-wide for days
  #518  loadConfig dropped the mount stamp, so baselining self-skipped
        everywhere and no run ever said so
  #555  a required manifest field landed with no migration; consumer packs
        stopped validating, and since a pack that fails validation
        contributes no rules, check_the_world kept reporting green about a
        corpus it was no longer running
  #424  five mounted skill links dangled on main, unnoticed

None was caught by canon CI, because the canon's own tree is always already
correct. All four would have fired on the first session after the change,
on the member, where the damage was.

Runs in three places. SessionStart, FIRST and report-only — never --strict
there, because a non-zero exit makes Claude Code discard the hook's stdout,
which would throw away the very report it exists to deliver. And baselining
preprocessing, against the just-converged tree, where a failure now
escalates to the agent: broken machinery is the judgment case, and merging
it would spread the breakage to a repo that was working an hour ago.

Pure probes over injected io, so the whole set runs with no tree on disk.
Not-applicable is a distinct result from failure throughout — conflating
them is how a check earns a reputation for crying wolf. Mutation-tested:
neutering the stamp probe and the hook-target probe each turn the suite red.

* claudinite: enforce the consumer-safe-change rule over the canon's own diff

Phase 4 of #593. consumer-safe-changes.md has always SAID that a change to
a vendored contract must carry consumers across it. Nothing enforced that,
and #555 merged green while eleven consumer packs stopped validating —
because the canon's own packs were updated in the same commit and canon CI
has nothing else to look at.

So this is a check over the diff, not prose about the diff. Work-scoped:
the branch's change is what it judges, and judging the whole tree would be
meaningless — the tree always contains a manifest field; the question is
whether THIS change added one.

Fires on three surfaces, each one a consumer holds a copy of and cannot be
asked to change in the same commit: pack-schema.mjs (#555's exact file), a
rule that is blocking, and the scheduler stub. Discharged by EITHER a
migration record or a rehearsal fixture — they answer different questions
('members are moved across' vs 'members are unharmed') and both are
legitimate; a genuinely additive change needs only the second.

Deliberately narrow. A rule that cried wolf on every canon commit would be
turned off within a week, and then be worth nothing on the day it mattered
— so ordinary engine and pack edits, advisory rules, and test files are all
untouched.

The fixture rehearsal is the fast gate; its honest weakness is that a
fixture only tests what someone remembered to model. The canary is the
other half: a REAL repo, really adopting Claudinite, converged against a
canon ref and asked whether it still works. Manual dispatch, plus
automatic on merge to main — post-merge is still much better than not
knowing, and #585 went two days unnoticed.

A DEDICATED disposable repo, not a real project: a rehearsal rewrites the
mount and can leave a failed converge behind, and pointing that at
EdFringeNow means a bad canon commit leaves a real project dirty exactly
when attention is elsewhere. The workflow no-ops with a warning until

the repo exists.

It runs the CANARY's own vendored worker, not this checkout's — that is
the copy a member runs, and testing anything else tests a path no consumer
ever executes.

Also makes the rehearsal fixtures independent of the HOST's git signing
config. They commit, and a machine with signing wired up fails those
commits for reasons unrelated to the canon change under test — the
rehearsal would then report a fleet-breaking result because a signing
helper was unavailable. Found exactly that way: this environment's signing
helper ran out of file descriptors mid-session.

part that answers 'with and without a migration': note selection fires

=== 710a07d prose-to-checks: gate conversion on product-vs-procedure (#596)
The convertibility test asked only whether a rule constrains a static
signature in the repo artifact. A statement of what the product does
passes that test easily — "this module must export X" has an obvious
signature — so the sweep could convert a requirement into a pack check,
splitting a feature's definition across two systems and landing half of
it where no test of the product ever reads it.

The rule that forbids this lived only in generate-project-instructions,
which the sweep never reads. Add it as an explicit first gate in the
prose-to-checks skill, ahead of the check-the-world test, and mirror it
in the sweep task's pick step and its never-do list. A product statement
found in pack prose is already mis-homed; the sweep leaves it and logs
it rather than cementing it as a check.

=== b08baeb basics: bar pinning and requirement-shaped rules from packs (#604)
* basics: bar pinning and requirement-shaped rules from packs (#603)

Two shapes of check keep being at risk of landing in a project's local
packs, and neither is a pack rule: one that asserts particular code
exists and still reads a particular way (a point-in-time pin — deleted
with the code it pins, constraining nothing about the next change), and
one derivable from the product's requirements (a requirement, whose home
is the requirements doc and the test that proves it).

The ladder lands this at prose: both are judgments about meaning with no
static signature, and both can leave a perfectly checkable signature, so
no check can separate them from a real convention. Stated once, in the
always-loaded baseline, so every authoring path has it in context:

- basics/RULES.md — the entry bar on the process-change ladder.
- prose-to-checks — its own test ("a static signature in the artifact?")
  answers yes for many requirement-shaped rules, so the sweep actively
  invited shape 2; the signature is now necessary, not sufficient.
- generate-project-instructions — the overlapping half of its
  requirement paragraph gives way to the baseline rule, keeping the
  discriminating residue (recognizing a requirement in convention's
  clothes).

=== 0ab6325 Commit-separation rule, and the three defects the deletion-test sweep surfaced (#560)
* Rule: unrelated concerns in one PR get one commit each

A commit is the unit of one task. Two fixes that could each stand alone —
each revertible, cherry-pickable, bisectable on its own — never share one.
The layering rules beside it order a single task's work; this one keeps
separate tasks from being layered together at all.

Ladder triage put it at the skill rung: a setting, a hook, or a check would
each have to judge whether two edits belong to the same task, which is
meaning rather than signature. feature-requirements-first can check an
ordering because both its ends are identifiable artifacts; "unrelated" has
no such tell, and a check guessing at it would fire on every broad change.

The corpus did not already carry it. The layering section covers one task's
internal order (failing test before implementation, docs after); the
"don't improve unrelated rules while you're in there" bounds on the growth
tasks scope what a run may touch, and say nothing about committing work
that legitimately does land together.

=== 005edd2 Scheduler: fail closed on an unreadable run ledger, narrow the first-run fan-out (#523)
The due-slot watermark is the last successful scheduler run, read from the
Actions ledger. Two defects sat on that read.

`lastSuccessTime` returned null on any non-200, and `dueSlots` reads null as
"fresh adoption → fire everything". So a rate limit, a 5xx or a token blip on a
mature repo re-fired every frequency off-anchor, silently. null is not "no
data" here — it is a positive claim that the repo has never run, so the read now
returns it only for a 200 that found no successful run, and throws otherwise
(including a run record carrying no timestamp, the same conflation by a narrower
route). The run then exits non-zero rather than evaluating: a failed run never
enters the success ledger, so the watermark stays put and the next successful run
catches up the missed slots. An exit-0 abort would instead advance the watermark
past the slots it declined to evaluate.

The first-run fan-out is now hourly plus the daily family, never weekly or
monthly. The first run is an adoption smoke test, and the wiring it proves —
discovery, signals, dispatch issue, label, executor pickup — is identical
whatever the frequency, so the daily family exercises all of it. Weekly and
monthly only added an off-anchor run of their unconditional tasks (open-web
research, pack discovery, the fleet sweep) on the least-proven repo in the
fleet; they wait for their real anchor, which is due normally once the first run
is in the ledger.

=== ea5b0ef Executor: read the CCR trigger, and never guess an issue (#511)
The executor identified its one dispatch from `$GITHUB_EVENT_PATH` alone.
GitHub Actions writes that file; Claude Code on the web does not — it
delivers the same `[REDACTED:env:CCR_TRIGGER_EVENT]` trigger as `CCR_TRIGGER_*` environment
variables. So every CCR-run executor session missed its own trigger, hit
the no-payload exit, and took the documented fallback: list the ready
label, pick the oldest.

That fallback is the duplicate-execution bug reached from the other
direction. One scheduler run files every due dispatch seconds apart, so
every session that cannot name its trigger builds the *same* work list and
races the others over it; the claim in step 2 cannot save them because they
all read the list before any of them claims. Observed live 2026-07-28:
dispatch #772 selected by two sessions and claimed one second apart.

Two changes, both needed — teaching the shell the second transport removes
the cause, deleting the fallback removes the failure mode:

- `resolve-dispatch.mjs` now resolves its trigger from either transport.
  The Actions payload still answers in one shot. A CCR trigger names the
  issue but carries neither its labels nor its body, so it resolves in two:
  exit 13 `needs-issue` prints the number, the executor fetches that one

=== ac24444 A project can declare itself dormant (#561)
* Let a project declare itself dormant, and honour it fleet-wide

A finished or parked project should not keep paying the upkeep of one that is
being worked on. It now says so in its own declaration:

    "dormant": true

The scheduler reads that FIRST, ahead of the due-slot math and every task's own
precondition, and stops: no task evaluated, no signal collected, no dispatch
issue filed or maintained, no agent session, no maintenance PR. One gate covers
every task, canon and local, present and future — no task declaration mentions
dormancy, and FORCE_TASKS does not reach past it (forcing overrides a
precondition; dormancy is not one). Slots are skipped, not deferred: the run
still exits 0 so the watermark advances and waking a project does not replay the
months it slept through.

Dormancy is narrow on purpose. It switches off recurring, unattended work only —
sessions, hooks, checks, skills and pack prose are untouched.

The fleet honours it with the SAME predicate, re-exported from the engine rather
than re-tested, so the enforcer and a member's own scheduler can never disagree:
- freshness skips a dormant member before reading its stamp and closes any open
  drift issue `not planned` — its scheduler is stopped, so the mount falls behind
  by design, and reporting that is nagging a repo for obeying its declaration;
- usage drops it from the denominator and names it under `coverage.dormant`,
  since a silent repo says nothing about whether a skill earns its place;
- the census is deliberately unchanged: a dormant repo is still a member.

Closes #562

=== 45090dc Executor CCR start: one-step --issue-json handshake and a quotable Task brief (#550)
The CCR start of an executor session took five judgment-laden steps: run
resolve-dispatch (exit 13), fetch the issue over MCP, hand-extract the body
into a file, hand-assemble a labels CSV, re-run with two flags. The two
extraction steps were pure mechanics an agent can fumble, and nothing
verified the fetched issue was the one the trigger named.

resolve-dispatch.mjs now takes --issue-json <path>: the executor saves the
raw MCP issue-get response verbatim and the shell extracts body, labels, and
title itself — accepting both label shapes (MCP strings, REST {name}
objects) — and refuses in code a response whose number differs from the
trigger's. The manual --issue-body-file/--issue-labels pair stays as the
fallback.

Exit 0 additionally prints a slot: field (parsed from the dispatch title,
which both the Actions payload and --issue-json carry) and a one-line
brief: ("Task: <pack>/<task> (slot ...) — issue #N, model M, outcome
ceiling O, timeout Ts") that executor.md now requires quoting prominently
in chat before the claim, so a human skimming a session sees at a glance
which task ran and under what parameters.

Both new guards are mutation-checked: disabling the wrong-issue refusal or
the {name} label normalization each fails its test.

=== 939929a Usage metrics: count check activations and every check failure (#545)
* Usage metrics: count check activations and every check failure (#544)

The fold already counts skill loads. It now counts the conformance checks
too — and the failures above all: a check that fails is a win, because the
finding reaches the session through the Stop hook and the agent corrects
before the work leaves the branch. Nothing measured that until now.

Neither runner writes a metrics file, so both are read off the marks they
already leave in the transcript, each by one tested function with a fixture
copied from a real capture:

  - the Stop hook's hooklog line, which reaches the transcript through hook
    stderr and is the ONLY mark a passing run leaves — the reason work-scope
    RUNS are countable, not just failures. Its reason also carries the two
    outcomes nothing else reveals: a loop-guard relent (a failure that prints
    no findings block) and a runner-error (enforcement silently off);
  - report-findings' summary line, which names its own scope and survives the
    `| tail` an agent usually pipes a run through — printed only when there
    were findings, so it counts failures, never runs;
  - the runner's Bash invocation, which is how the world scope runs at all.

Runs come only from the marks a passing run also leaves; where a test command
wraps the runner without naming it, the summary lines are the floor — the count
is the max of the two signals, never their sum. One hook execution recorded
under two entry shapes dedupes on its hooklog stamp, because a doubled failure
count is precisely the number that must not be inflated. Only Bash results are
read, paired back to their command: in the corpus that owns the runners,
reading a file that merely mentions this vocabulary is the ordinary case.

Per repo the day and week rows gain `checks` (per scope: runs, failures,
errors, blocking, advisory) and `checkFindings` (per rule); the sheepdog
sweep carries both at the same week x repo grain, since whether a rule earns
its place is a fleet question exactly as a skill's is. A week folded before
this shipped grows from the day it closes forward rather than wedging the
watermark, and a member still on the older fold lands as an empty check row.

Every check number is a floor: a world sweep that ran in CI left no mark in
any session. The under-count is one-directional by construction, and stated
in the fleet file's own _note.

* Usage metrics: count CI checks when the agent was in the loop on them (#544)

Write, commit, let CI run, fix what it caught is the same correction loop as
the Stop hook's, one turn wider — so a CI check failure the session acted on
is the same kind of win, and the first pass counted none of them. It counts
exactly when the session PULLED THE JOB LOG IN, which is what "the agent was
in the loop" means operationally. A nightly or post-merge run nobody looked at
stays uncounted, correctly: nothing was corrected.

Three things stood between the marks and a fetched CI log, each verified
against a real captured payload rather than assumed:

  - the log arrives through a CI-log tool, not Bash. Matched by name shape
    (job/run/workflow _logs) so a different server or a rename still lands;
  - an MCP tool returns its payload as a JSON DOCUMENT inside a text block, so
    the log's newlines arrive ESCAPED. Every mark here is line-anchored, so
    left encoded the whole job log is ONE line and the counting silently
    measures nothing — the failure mode that reads as "CI never catches
    anything". Decoded by parsing and joining the string leaves, which needs
    no field name and so holds for whichever tool delivers the log;
